P01.quote: It's not that it makes things up all the time, but when it does, it's convincing.
Last month it wrote that a patient had denied chest pain, and we never discussed chest pain at all.
I treat it like a draft from a student.
For the complicated ones, the frail older patient with six problems, I sometimes turn it off and write the assessment myself.
P01.rationale: Keeps clinical reasoning for complex cases.

P01.quote: I'd say I've gained back something like forty-five minutes a day, maybe an hour on a heavy clinic day.
A few people have asked who else can hear it, which is a fair question.
P01.rationale: Questions about who can access recordings.

P01.quote: The formatting sometimes breaks, bullet points turn into one long paragraph, and the medication list doesn't land in the medication field, so I retype it.
P01.rationale: Formatting problems moving drafts into the record.
The tool is easy to start.

P02.quote: Our medical director made the decision, and I made it happen.
When the doubters see a colleague leaving on time, that does more than any presentation from me.
What actually worked was our own lunch-and-learn, where Dr. Okafor showed her real workflow on a test patient.
It took six weeks to get written answers.
P02.rationale: Slow vendor responses to privacy questions.

P02.quote: A written agreement that audio is deleted after the note is generated, that our data isn't used for training, and that processing happens in Canada.
The licence isn't cheap, and it's per clinician per month.
patients sometimes ask them about it before they see the doctor, and they weren't prepared for those questions at first.
P02.rationale: Patients raise consent questions at the front desk.

P02.quote: the copying back and forth is the number one complaint I hear.
P02.rationale: Main complaint is moving drafts into the record.

P03.quote: Some people ask if it's like a smart speaker that's always listening.
Nobody had told us much, it was mainly the doctors who got trained.
Usually they tell me, and I put a little flag on their appointment so the doctor knows before they walk in.
Before, the last appointments would run late because they were catching up on charts between patients.
P03.rationale: Charting delayed afternoon appointments before adoption.

P03.quote: They say "I guess it's fine" in a voice that doesn't sound fine.
When the phone app doesn't work, the doctor sometimes comes out to the desk to ask for a charger or for help, and I'm not tech support.
And maybe have the information sheet in more languages.

P04.quote: The regional health authority offered it to a handful of community clinics as part of a pilot.
P04.rationale: How the tool reached the clinic.

P04.quote: It's good at the medical parts: symptoms, medications, the plan.
If someone tells me they're sleeping in their car this week, that's the most important thing in the visit, and the draft might mention it in one line at the bottom, or leave it out entirely.
With others, especially people who've had bad experiences with institutions, the idea that something is listening changes the conversation.
P04.rationale: Recording changes conversations with some patients.

P04.quote: Partly for the patient's comfort, partly because I'm not confident enough about where that audio goes, even with what we've been told.
Our policy is basically "use your professional judgement," which I appreciate, but it puts it back on us.
It also doesn't know our templates, so the structure of the draft doesn't match the structure our charts are supposed to follow.
P04.rationale: Drafts do not match chart templates.

P04.quote: For straightforward visits, yes, maybe ten minutes each.
Another NP and I made our own cheat sheet and shared it around.

P05.quote: I found errors in about one note out of five.
a dose recorded wrong, laterality flipped, left knee instead of right
But one note said I'd examined a patient's abdomen when I hadn't.
So for me the time savings didn't materialise.
If something is right ninety percent of the time, your attention drifts.
I've asked our residents not to use it during their first year with us, and our program director supports that for now.
One patient asked me directly whether the company would use her conversation to improve its product, and I couldn't give her a confident answer at the time.
To her credit she took it seriously and asked the health authority for clearer answers about data use.
If someone showed me that it was as accurate as a good human scribe, I'd use it tomorrow.

P06.quote: The first time, I didn't really understand what I was agreeing to.
She looked at me the whole time. I felt like she was really hearing me, instead of half-listening while she typed.
honestly that visit was one of the best I've had.
the tool itself made the visit better, but the way I was asked made me feel less in control.
I wondered afterwards whether saying no meant I got a worse appointment.
We heard about it from patients asking questions in the waiting room.
